Dear Dr. Morrison,

Thank you for seeing Leo Davies, a 3-year-old boy, for a comprehensive neurological assessment.

Leo's symptoms began at 7 months of age when he experienced his first convulsive episode during a high fever. Since that initial febrile convulsion, he has experienced several generalized bilateral tonic-clonic seizures. Importantly, these events appear generalized from the start, with no witnessed focal onset prior to the bilateral motor activity. His parents report no other seizure semiologies; they have observed no focal motor spells, focal aware events, or focal seizures with impaired awareness. We have also seen no signs of non-motor absence episodes, sudden atonic drops, myoclonic jerks, or isolated tonic posturing.

Leo was born at full term following an uncomplicated pregnancy, and his immunizations are up to date. His developmental milestones have all been achieved on schedule, with no signs of global developmental delay. He is conversational, socially engaging, and his general physical and cranial nerve examinations today were entirely unremarkable.

Recent investigations include an electroencephalogram, which showed definitive epileptiform abnormalities. A subsequent brain MRI demonstrated age-appropriate CNS myelination with well-preserved cerebral white matter volume and no evidence of diffuse cerebral atrophy. The corpus callosum demonstrates normal thickness, the cerebellar vermis shows no hypoplasia, and the bilateral hippocampi are intact without sclerosis.

He is currently not on daily anticonvulsants, though rectal diazepam was supplied as a rescue medication. I would appreciate your expert recommendations regarding his assessment and ongoing management.

Warm regards,
Dr. Eleanor Vance
